consensus_explanation.summary: IDEAL tested a causal mechanism (HMGCR inhibition lowering LDL-C) against an active statin comparator, so the achievable contrast was small: the design expected about 40 mg/dL (1 mmol/L) LDL-C separation and a 21% risk reduction, but the arms differed by only ~23 mg/dL (0.55-0.59 mmol/L), with ~77% of patients already on statins, simvastatin titrated to 40 mg in 21%, atorvastatin 80 mg lowering LDL-C less than expected (49% in statin-naive patients) and twice as many discontinuations. The investigators attributed the non-significant 11% reduction in major coronary events (HR 0.89, 0.78-1.01, P=0.07) mainly to an LDL-C difference 'slightly smaller than projected' and to follow-up length, while broader composites were reduced (major cardiovascular events HR 0.87, nonfatal MI HR 0.83, any coronary event HR 0.84). The observed effect matches what the LDL hypothesis predicts for ~0.55 mmol/L: CTT 2010 pooled IDEAL with PROVE-IT, A to Z, TNT and SEARCH (0.51 mmol/L further reduction, 15% fewer major vascular events, proportional to the LDL-C difference), and Cannon's 2006 meta-analysis of TNT, IDEAL, PROVE IT and A to Z found a 16% reduction in coronary death or MI. So the field reads IDEAL as an underpowered confirmation of 'lower is better' rather than evidence against the mechanism. Contributing design issues: effect-size assumption too optimistic for the achievable contrast, a narrow coronary-only primary end point, and the open-label PROBE design.
